posts.title: The Lamp Stays Lit
posts.body:
I kept a lamp beside the window,
not for the road, not for the rain,
but for the words that come at midnight
and will not knock twice.

They sit with me like old neighbours,
shoes left at the door,
speaking of things the day was too loud
to let me hear.

By morning they are gone again.
Only the oil is lower,
and the page, which was empty,
remembers everything.

posts.title: On Unsent Letters
posts.body:
Some letters are not meant to be posted. Writing them is the whole journey; the envelope was only ever a place to keep the courage.

I have a drawer of them. Each one is a door I closed gently instead of slamming.

posts.title: रास्ते ने पूछा
posts.body:
रास्ते ने पूछा, कहाँ तक चलोगे?
मैंने कहा, जहाँ तक तुम ले चलो।

पैरों में थकान है, आँखों में सुबह,
मंज़िल अभी दूर है, पर चलना अच्छा लगता है।

posts.title: The Tailor of Anarkali
posts.body:
In a lane so narrow that two bicycles had to negotiate like diplomats, there was a tailor who never measured anyone. Customers would stand before him with their arms out, waiting for the yellow tape, and he would only look at them for a long moment, the way one looks at weather.

“You walk as though you are carrying something heavy on your left side,” he told a schoolteacher once. She laughed and said it was only her bag of exercise books. When the kurta came back, the left shoulder had been cut a little wider, and for the first time in years she did not feel her coat pulling her toward the ground.

People said he was guessing. His apprentice, a boy named Faraz who swept the floor and threaded needles faster than anyone in the bazaar, knew better. The old man was listening. He listened to how a person stood when they thought no one was watching, to the half-step a man took before he spoke to his father, to the way a bride held her hands as if they belonged to someone else.

One winter evening, when the gas heaters hissed and the lane smelled of roasted peanuts, a stranger came in and asked for a coat that would make him look important. The tailor looked at him for longer than usual. Then he set down his scissors.

“I can make you a coat,” he said. “But it will only fit the man who walks out of here, not the one who walked in. Come back when you know which one you want to be.”

The stranger left without a word. Faraz thought that was the end of it. But in spring the man returned, quieter, his shoulders lower, and this time he did not ask for anything at all. He simply stood with his arms out and waited, and the old tailor, smiling, reached for the yellow tape.
